docs.title: 1. Set Up Raspberry Pi OS
docs.text: Using Raspberry Pi ImagerUsing Rufus (Windows)Using dd (Linux / macOS)

docs.title: Install Raspberry Pi Imager<sup>1</sup>
docs.text:
Download the installer for your computer's OS from https://www.raspberrypi.com/software/.

  • Windows: run the downloaded imager_*.exe and follow the installer.
  • macOS: open the downloaded imager_*.dmg and drag Raspberry Pi Imager into Applications.

  • Linux (x86_64): make the downloaded AppImage executable, then run it in the terminal:

    chmod +x imager_*_amd64.AppImage
./imager_*_amd64.AppImage

docs.title: Insert the microSD card
docs.text: Insert the microSD card into your computer's card slot, or into a USB card reader connected to the computer.

docs.title: Select the device
docs.text: On the Device tab, select your Raspberry Pi model, then select Next.

docs.title: Select the operating system
docs.text:
On the OS tab, select the operating system, then select Next.

What OS do I need to install?

If you have a Raspberry Pi 4, 4B, etc., and want the benefit of a graphical interface, choose the recommended Raspberry Pi OS (64-bit).

If you have a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, or wish to run it as a headless server, go to Raspberry Pi OS (Other) > select Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit).

For other devices, choose the one with the corresponding architecture.

docs.title: Select the storage
docs.text: On the Storage tab, select the microSD card, then select Next. Identify the card by its size, and keep Exclude system drives turned on to avoid erasing your computer's own drive by mistake.

docs.title: Customize the OS (recommended)
docs.text:
This step is recommended to skip first-time customization during boot. It is a necessary step if you wish to use this Raspberry Pi headless without peripherals.

  • Hostname: enter a name using only letters, numbers and hyphens. Other devices can reach the Pi at <hostname>.local.
  • Localisation: choose a capital city. Imager fills in the time zone and keyboard layout, which you can change separately. The city also sets the Wi-Fi regulatory domain.
  • User: enter a username and password. The username must be lowercase and can contain letters, numbers, underscores and hyphens.

  • Wi-Fi: choose a secure or open network and enter the SSID. For a secure network, enter the password. Turn on Hidden SSID if the network doesn't broadcast its name.

    Note

    eduroam requires separate logins and certificates on top of the SSID and password. It cannot be configured via Raspberry Pi Imager.

    It can be configured later in the terminal, but the Pi needs another way to connect first:

    • Another Wi-Fi network, such as a home network or a phone hotspot, entered in the Wi-Fi settings above
    • An Ethernet cable connected to a router
    • A keyboard and monitor connected directly to the Pi

    Consult the IT department for the eduroam settings and certificate at your institution.

  • Remote Access: turn on Enable SSH, then choose password authentication or public key authentication. For a public key, paste it in or select Browse to find the key file.

docs.title: Write the image and validate
docs.text:
After all settings are configured, you can review a summary of your choices in the Writing tab. If this information is correct, select Write in the bottom-right corner of Imager. When Imager warns that all data on the card will be erased, select I understand, erase and write. If you see a prompt asking for administrator permission, grant the permissions to proceed.

This process will take a few minutes based on the speed of the card reader you are using.

docs.title: Finish
docs.text: When the Done tab appears, select Finish and remove the microSD card.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: 1. https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/getting-started.html ↩

docs.title: Update the package list
docs.text:
sudo apt update

This downloads the latest list of available packages and versions. It doesn't install anything yet.

docs.title: Upgrade the installed packages
docs.text:
sudo apt full-upgrade

When prompted Do you want to continue? [Y/n], press Y and then Enter. This also updates the Linux kernel and firmware. Use full-upgrade rather than upgrade, because Raspberry Pi OS changes package dependencies more often than Debian does.1

Not enough disk space?

If full-upgrade reports that it needs more space, check your free space with:

df -h

To make room, delete old downloaded package files with:

sudo apt clean

docs.title: Reboot
docs.text: sudo reboot

docs.text: 1. https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/computers/os.html ↩

docs.title: 3. Configure zram
docs.text: Since Raspberry Pi OS Trixie (released 2 October 2025), zram is built in. The rpi-swap package sets up compressed swap on /dev/zram0 automatically at boot.1 The zram-tools method sets up its own zram swap and conflicts with rpi-swap. Instead, configure zram with a drop-in file as shown below.

docs.title: Remove zram-tools (optional)
docs.text:
If you tried installing zram-tools, run:

sudo apt purge zram-tools

docs.title: Drop-in file structure
docs.text:
rpi-swap reads its defaults from /etc/rpi/swap.conf. To avoid your changes being overridden and accidentally breaking setups, create a drop-in file in /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/ instead of editing the main file. Drop-ins override the main file and are read in filename order. If more than one drop-in sets the same property, the file read last takes precedence. The 90- prefix makes 90-local.conf load after lower-numbered files.2

A drop-in has up to three sections. Include only the sections and properties you want to change; everything else keeps its default.

[Main]
Mechanism=...

[Zram]
FixedSizeMiB=...

[File]
FixedSizeMiB=...

docs.title: [Main]
docs.text: Property Values Default Meaning Mechanism auto, swapfile, zram, zram+file, none auto Which kind of swap to use. auto lets rpi-swap choose. zram+file uses compressed RAM and writes idle pages to a file on disk. zram uses RAM only. swapfile is a traditional swap file. none disables swap.

docs.title: [Zram]
docs.text: Property Default Meaning RamMultiplier 1 zram capacity as a multiple of your RAM. 1 means a capacity equal to your RAM. MaxSizeMiB 2048 Upper limit on the size that RamMultiplier calculates FixedSizeMiB (unset) Exact capacity in MiB. Overrides RamMultiplier and MaxSizeMiB. WritebackTrigger auto How idle pages are moved to the file: timer, manual or auto. auto lets rpi-swap choose. WritebackInitialDelay 180min Wait after boot before the first writeback WritebackPeriodicInterval 24h Time between writebacks

docs.title: [File]
docs.text:
The file at /var/swap stores the idle pages that zram writes back.

Property Default Meaning Path /var/swap Location of the file RamMultiplier 1 File size as a multiple of your RAM MaxSizeMiB 2048 Upper limit on the file size MaxDiskPercent 50 Upper limit as a percentage of available disk space FixedSizeMiB (unset) Exact file size in MiB. Overrides the settings above.

docs.title: Choosing a size
docs.text:
FixedSizeMiB is how much data zram can hold before compression. Because zram compresses that data 2–3×, a full zram uses much less real RAM:

Real RAM used when full ≈ FixedSizeMiB ÷ 2 to 3

For example, a full 8192 MiB (8 GB) zram uses about 8 ÷ 3 to 8 ÷ 2 ≈ 2.7–4 GB of real RAM.

This is a chart of suggested zram size versus real RAM used when full. You can check your physical RAM size with:

free -h
Pi RAM Suggested FixedSizeMiB (1× RAM) Real RAM used when full 1 GB 1024 about 0.3–0.5 GB 2 GB 2048 about 0.7–1 GB 4 GB 4096 about 1.3–2 GB 8 GB 8192 about 2.7–4 GB 16 GB 16384 about 5.3–8 GB

Warning

Values above 2× your RAM are not recommended, because poorly compressible data could then fill all of your memory.2 This will thrash the system instead of benefiting it.

docs.title: Create the drop-in
docs.text:
The example below is for an 8 GB Pi. Replace 8192 with the value for your Pi from the table above, and replace the parameters with those of your choice.

Create the directory and open the drop-in in nano:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d
sudo nano /etc/rpi/swap.conf.d/90-local.conf

Using nano

nano is a simple text editor that runs in the terminal. Type or paste the text, then press Ctrl+O and Enter to save, and Ctrl+X to exit.

Add these lines:

[Main]
Mechanism=zram+file

[Zram]
FixedSizeMiB=8192

(Optional) To make the file at /var/swap larger than its 2 GB default, add a [File] section with its own FixedSizeMiB to the same file, for example:

[File]
FixedSizeMiB=4096

docs.title: Reload system service
docs.text: sudo systemctl daemon-reload

docs.title: Verify the configuration
docs.text:
After reloading, run:

zramctl
swapon --show

You should see /dev/zram0 using zstd, with DISKSIZE matching the size you set (8G in the example above). You don't need to set zstd anywhere: it's already in use, and rpi-swap has no setting for the algorithm.

Advanced: Kernel parameters to make better use of zram

The Linux kernel can be tuned and tweaked to make better use of zram.5

docs.title: Kernel parameters<sup>4</sup>
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning vm.swappiness 60 The relative I/O cost of swapping compared with dropping file cache, from 0 to 200. At 100, both are treated as equally costly. Higher values make the kernel prefer swapping. For in-memory swap such as zram, values above 100 can be considered. vm.page-cluster 3 How many consecutive pages are read from swap at once, as a power of 2 (3 = 8 pages). 0 reads one page at a time, which disables swap readahead and lowers latency. rpi-swap already sets this to 0. vm.vfs_cache_pressure 100 How readily the kernel reclaims memory used to cache directory and inode objects. Higher values reclaim it sooner; lower values keep it longer. 0 never reclaims it and can easily lead to out-of-memory conditions. Values significantly above 100 may hurt performance. vm.dirty_background_ratio 10 The percentage of available memory that can hold "dirty" pages (modified data not yet written to disk) before background threads start writing them to disk. vm.dirty_ratio 20 The percentage of available memory that can hold dirty pages before a process that is writing to disk must write them out itself. vm.watermark_boost_factor 15000 How much extra memory the kernel reclaims when memory becomes fragmented, in units of 1/10,000 of the high watermark (15000 = 150%). 0 disables this. vm.watermark_scale_factor 10 How early the background reclaim thread (kswapd) wakes up, in units of 1/10,000 of memory (10 = 0.1%). The maximum is 3000 (30%). Higher values start reclaiming earlier.

To check a value on your Pi, run sysctl with the parameter name, for example:

sysctl vm.swappiness

Note

Debian 13 (and Raspberry Pi OS Trixie) no longer reads /etc/sysctl.conf. Put kernel parameters in a file under /etc/sysctl.d/ instead.3

docs.title: Create the configuration file
docs.text:
Create /etc/sysctl.d/99-zram.conf with sudo nano /etc/sysctl.d/99-zram.conf and add these lines:

vm.vfs_cache_pressure = 500
vm.swappiness = 100
vm.dirty_background_ratio = 1
vm.dirty_ratio = 50
vm.watermark_boost_factor = 0
vm.watermark_scale_factor = 125
vm.page-cluster = 0

docs.title: Apply the parameters
docs.text:
Reboot your system, or enable the new parameters with:

sudo sysctl --system

docs.title: 4. Create a Second Network Interface (Optional)
docs.text:
A second network interface lets the Pi connect to two networks at once: the mesh network and a Wi-Fi network (WLAN). You need it to:

  • Host what's inside the mesh network on the WLAN, so that devices on the Wi-Fi network can reach services running inside the mesh network.
  • Access the internet via the WLAN and share it inside the mesh network, so that devices in the mesh network can get online through the Pi.
Using a Plug-and-Play Wi-Fi DongleUsing an ESP32 DevKit via GPIO

A plug-and-play dongle has its driver built into the Linux kernel, so it works without installing anything.

ESP-Hosted-Linux1 turns an ESP32 DevKit into a Wi-Fi interface for the Pi. The DevKit runs the ESP-Hosted-Linux firmware, and a driver on the Pi shows it as a normal Wi-Fi interface that NetworkManager can manage.

Warning

Raspberry Pi GPIO pins use 3.3 V logic. Do not connect ESP signals to 5 V pins.

ESP-Hosted-Linux supports these chips:2

Chip Wi-Fi Transport Bluetooth Thread / 802.15.4 ESP32 2.4 GHz, b/g/n SDIO (see the warning below), SPI Classic + BLE — ESP32-S2 2.4 GHz, b/g/n SPI — — ESP32-S3 2.4 GHz, b/g/n SPI BLE — ESP32-S31 2.4 GHz, b/g/n SPI, USB Classic + BLE Yes (on by default in firmware) ESP32-C2 2.4 GHz, b/g/n SPI BLE — ESP32-C3 2.4 GHz, b/g/n SPI BLE — ESP32-C5 2.4 / 5 GHz, a/b/g/n/ac/ax SDIO, SPI BLE — ESP32-C6 2.4 GHz, b/g/n/ax SDIO, SPI BLE Yes (must be enabled in firmware) ESP32-C61 2.4 GHz, b/g/n/ax SDIO, SPI BLE —

ESP32 over SDIO

On ESP32 modules and DevKits with 3.3 V flash, such as the ESP32-DevKitC, GPIO12 (MTDI) selects the flash voltage and must be pulled low at reset. SDIO needs a pull-up on DAT2, which is GPIO12, so the two are incompatible. The fix is to burn an eFuse, which can't be undone. Read Conflicts Between Bootstrap and SDIO on DAT2 before using SDIO with an ESP32.

docs.title: Plug in the dongle
docs.text: Plug the Wi-Fi dongle into a USB port on the Pi.

docs.title: Find the new interface
docs.text:
nmcli device

A new wifi device appears, usually named wlan1. Use this name in the next steps. If no new wifi device appears, the dongle's driver is not built in, and the dongle is not plug-and-play on Raspberry Pi OS.

docs.title: Wire the DevKit to the Pi<sup>3</sup>
docs.text:
SPISDIO Function ESP32 ESP32-S2/S3 ESP32-S31 ESP32-C2/C3/C5/C6 ESP32-C61 Pi physical pin CS IO15 IO10 IO23 IO10 IO8 24 SCLK IO14 IO12 IO20 IO6 IO6 23 MISO IO12 IO13 IO22 IO2 IO2 21 MOSI IO13 IO11 IO21 IO7 IO7 19 Handshake IO2 IO2 IO3 IO3 IO3 15 Data Ready IO4 IO4 IO4 IO4 IO4 13 Reset EN RST RST RST RST 31 Ground GND GND GND GND GND 25

CS requires a pull-up of at least 10 kΩ to 3.3 V, which keeps the line from floating during reset or boot.

Function ESP32 ESP32-C5 ESP32-C6 ESP32-C61 Pi physical pin DAT3 IO13 IO13 IO23 IO23 13 CLK IO14 IO9 IO19 IO26 15 CMD IO15 IO10 IO18 IO25 16 DAT0 IO2 IO8 IO20 IO27 18 DAT1 IO4 IO7 IO21 IO28 22 DAT2 IO12 IO14 IO22 IO22 37 Reset EN RST RST RST 31 Ground GND GND GND GND 39

CMD and DAT0–DAT3 require 10 kΩ pull-ups. Keep the wires below 10 cm, and avoid putting the SDIO jumper wires too close together. Otherwise both capacitance and mutual capacitance increase, which causes signal degradation and crosstalk, or, in severe cases, stops SDIO from working at all.

Warning

On an ESP32, read the "ESP32 over SDIO" warning above before fitting the pull-up on DAT2 (IO12).

docs.title: Install the ESP-IDF prerequisites
docs.text:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git wget flex bison gperf python3 python3-pip python3-venv cmake ninja-build ccache libffi-dev libssl-dev dfu-util libusb-1.0-0

docs.title: Download ESP-Hosted-Linux
docs.text:
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/espressif/esp-hosted-linux.git

docs.title: Prepare ESP-IDF<sup>4</sup>
docs.text:
cd ~/esp-hosted-linux/esp/esp_driver
./setup.sh
. ./esp-idf/export.sh

docs.title: Build and flash the firmware
docs.text:
cd network_adapter
idf.py set-target <target>
idf.py menuconfig

Replace <target> with your chip's name in lowercase without the hyphen, e.g. esp32c5. For the ESP32-S31, use idf.py --preview set-target esp32s31 instead.

In the menu, go to Example Configuration > Transport layer, select SPI interface or SDIO interface, then save and exit using the keys shown at the bottom of the menu.

Connect the DevKit to a USB port on the Pi with a USB cable, then find its serial port:

ls /dev/ttyUSB* /dev/ttyACM*

Build and flash, replacing /dev/ttyUSB0 with the port you found:

idf.py -p /dev/ttyUSB0 build flash

docs.title: Configure the Pi
docs.text:
sudo nano /boot/firmware/config.txt

Add this line at the end, then save and exit:

SPISDIO 
dtparam=spi=on

dtoverlay=sdio,poll_once=off

Reboot to apply it:

sudo reboot

docs.title: Build and load the driver
docs.text:
cd ~/esp-hosted-linux/host
SPISDIO 
./rpi_init.sh spi

./rpi_init.sh sdio

docs.title: Find the new interface
docs.text:
nmcli device

A new wifi device appears, usually named wlan1. Use this name in the next steps.

docs.title: Load the driver at boot
docs.text:
Create a service that loads the driver at every boot:

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/esp-hosted-linux.service

Add these lines. Replace <username> with your username, and replace spi with sdio if you use SDIO:

[Unit]
Description=ESP-Hosted-Linux driver

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
Environment=ESP_HOSTED_INCREMENTAL=1
ExecStart=/home/<username>/esp-hosted-linux/host/rpi_init.sh spi

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

ESP_HOSTED_INCREMENTAL=1 makes the script reuse the driver you built in the previous step instead of building it again. It only recompiles when something has changed, such as after a kernel update.

Enable the service and reboot:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable esp-hosted-linux.service
sudo reboot

After the reboot, check that the service ran and that wlan1 is back:

systemctl status esp-hosted-linux.service
nmcli device

To reload the driver later, run sudo systemctl restart esp-hosted-linux.service.

docs.title: Connect to the Wi-Fi network
docs.text:
These steps use wlan1. Replace it with your interface name if it's different.

List the networks the interface can see:

nmcli device wifi list ifname wlan1

Connect to your network, replacing <SSID> and <password> with its name and password:

sudo nmcli device wifi connect "<SSID>" password "<password>" ifname wlan1

NetworkManager saves the connection and reconnects automatically after a reboot.

docs.title: Verify the connection
docs.text:
nmcli device

wlan1 should show connected, followed by the network name.

(Optional) Create a profile for quicker connection

A profile stores a network's settings under a name of your choice, so you can connect with a single command.

docs.title: Profile properties<sup>5</sup>
docs.text:
Wi-Fi networks are either Personal (one shared password, e.g. home Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot) or Enterprise (a personal login, e.g. eduroam or a company network).

Property Used for What to fill in con-name All networks A name for the profile, used later to connect ifname All networks The interface to use, e.g. wlan1 ssid All networks The name of the Wi-Fi network wifi-sec.key-mgmt All networks The security type: wpa-psk for Personal networks, wpa-eap for Enterprise networks wifi-sec.psk Personal The Wi-Fi password 802-1x.eap Enterprise The EAP authentication method, e.g. peap or ttls 802-1x.phase2-auth Enterprise The inner authentication method, e.g. mschapv2 802-1x.identity Enterprise Your login, usually your institutional username or email address 802-1x.anonymous-identity Enterprise The outer identity, sent unencrypted, e.g. anonymous@<institution-domain> 802-1x.password Enterprise Your institutional password 802-1x.ca-cert Enterprise The path to your institution's CA certificate 802-1x.domain-suffix-match Enterprise The domain name of your institution's authentication server

docs.title: Example 1: Regular home Wi-Fi
docs.text:
sudo nmcli connection add type wifi ifname wlan1 con-name <profile> ssid "<SSID>" \
  wifi-sec.key-mgmt wpa-psk \
  wifi-sec.psk "<password>"

docs.title: Example 2: eduroam
docs.text:
sudo nmcli connection add type wifi ifname wlan1 con-name <profile> ssid eduroam \
  wifi-sec.key-mgmt wpa-eap \
  802-1x.eap peap \
  802-1x.phase2-auth mschapv2 \
  802-1x.identity "<username>" \
  802-1x.anonymous-identity "anonymous@<institution-domain>" \
  802-1x.password "<password>" \
  802-1x.ca-cert "<path-to-ca-cert>" \
  802-1x.domain-suffix-match "<server-domain>"

Note

The EAP method, inner authentication method, certificate and server domain differ between institutions. Consult the IT department for the eduroam settings and certificate at your institution.

docs.title: Connect with the profile
docs.text: sudo nmcli connection up <profile>
